source_text: Ἐπέταξε, φησὶν, ἔδει πεισθῆναι, καὶ μὴ τὸν δεῖνα προβάλλεσθαι, μηδὲ ἀλλότρια περιεργάζεσθαι κακά. Ἐπεὶ ὁ μέγας Δαυῒδ ἥμαρτεν ἁμαρτίαν χαλεπήν· ἆρα οὖν ἀκίνδυνον ἡμῖν διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν, εἰπέ μοι; Διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν τοῦτο ἀσφαλίζεσθαι χρὴ, καὶ τὰ κατορθώματα τῶν ἁγίων μόνον ζηλοῦν· εἰ δέ που ῥᾳθυμία καὶ νόμου παράβασις, μετὰ πολλῆς ἀποφεύγειν χρὴ τῆς σπουδῆς. Οὐ γὰρ πρὸς τοὺς συνδούλους ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν Δεσπότην ὁ λόγος ἐστὶ, καὶ τούτῳ τὰς εὐθύνας δώσομεν τῶν βεβιωμένων ἁπάντων. Πρὸς ἐκεῖνο τοίνυν παρασκευαζώμεθα τὸ δικαστήριον· κἂν γὰρ μυριάκις θαυμαστὸς ᾖ καὶ μέγας ὁ τὸν νόμον παραβαίνων τοῦτον, δώσει πάντως τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ παραβάσει κειμένην τιμωρίαν· οὐ γάρ ἐστι προσωπολήπτης ὁ Θεός. Πῶς οὖν ἔστι καὶ τίνι τρόπῳ φυγεῖν τὸ ἁμάρτημα; οὐ γὰρ δὴ μόνον τὸ ἔγκλημα χαλεπὸν χρὴ δεῖξαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅπως ἂν ἀπαλλαγείημεν συμβουλεῦσαι. Ἔχεις γυναῖκα, ἔχεις οἰκέτην, ἔχεις παιδία, καὶ φίλον, καὶ συγγενῆ, καὶ γείτονα; πᾶσι τούτοις τὴν ἐπὶ τούτων ἐπίτρεψον φυλακήν. Χαλεπὸν ἡ συνήθεια, καὶ δεινὸν ὑποσκελίσαι, καὶ δυσφύλακτον, καὶ ἄκοντας ἡμᾶς πολλάκις καὶ οὐκ εἰδότας ἐμβάλλει; Οὐκοῦν ὅσῳ τῆς συνηθείας οἶδας τὴν δύναμιν, τοσούτῳ τῆς μὲν πονηρᾶς συνηθείας ἀπαλλαγῆναι σπούδασον, πρὸς δὲ τὴν ἑτέραν τὴν χρησιμωτάτην σεαυτὸν μετάστησον. Ὥσπερ γὰρ νῦν σπουδάζοντά σε καὶ φυλαττόμενον καὶ μεριμνῶντα καὶ φροντίζοντα ἴσχυσε πολλάκις ὑποσκελίσαι ἐκείνη, οὕτως ἂν εἰς τὴν ἀγαθὴν σαυτὸν συνήθειαν μεταστήσῃς τὴν τοῦ μὴ ὀμνύναι, οὐδὲ ἄκων, οὐδὲ ῥᾳθυμῶν ἐμπεσεῖν δυνήσῃ ποτὲ πρὸς τὰ τῶν ὅρκων πτώματα· μέγα γὰρ ὄντως συνήθεια, καὶ φύσεως ἔχει δύναμιν. Ἵν' οὖν μὴ πονῶμεν συνεχῶς, ἑαυτοὺς εἰς συνήθειαν μεταστήσωμεν ἑτέραν, καὶ ἕκαστον τῶν σοι συγγινομένων καὶ συνόντων ταύτην αἴτησαι τὴν χάριν, ἵνα συμβουλεύῃ καὶ παραινῇ φεύγειν τοὺς ὅρκους, καὶ ἁλισκόμενον ἐλέγχῃ. Ἡ γὰρ παρ' αὐτῶν εἰς σὲ γινομένη φυλακὴ καὶ αὐτοῖς ἐστι συμβουλὴ καὶ παραίνεσις τοῦ κατορθώματος. Ὁ γὰρ ἐγκαλῶν ἑτέρῳ περὶ ὅρκων, οὐ ῥᾳδίως αὐτὸς εἰς τὸ βάραθρον ἐμπεσεῖται τοῦτο· βάραθρον γὰρ οὐ τὸ τυχὸν ἡ πολυορκία, οὐχ ὅταν περὶ τῶν ἐλαχίστων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὅταν περὶ μεγίστων γίνηται πραγμάτων. Ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ λάχανα ὠνούμενοι καὶ ὑπὲρ ὀβολῶν δύο φιλονεικοῦντες, καὶ πρὸς οἰκέτας ὀργιζόμενοι καὶ ἀπειλοῦντες, τὸν Θεὸν πανταχοῦ καλοῦμεν μάρτυρα· καὶ ἄνθρωπον μὲν ἐλεύθερον, ἀξίας τινὸς μετασχόντα ψιλῆς οὐκ ἂν ἐτόλμησας ὑπὲρ τοιούτων καλέσαι μάρτυρα ἐπ' ἀγορᾶς, ἀλλὰ κἂν ἐπιχειρήσῃς, δίκην δώσεις τῆς ὕβρεως· τὸν δὲ τῶν οὐρανῶν βασιλέα, τὸν τῶν ἀγγέλων Δεσπότην. καὶ περὶ ὠνίων, καὶ περὶ χρημάτων, καὶ περὶ τῶν τυχόντων διαλεγόμενος, ἕλκεις εἰς μαρτυρίαν· καὶ πῶς ταῦτα ἀνεκτά; Πόθεν οὖν ἀπαλλαγείημεν ἐκ τῆς πονηρᾶς ταύτης συνηθείας; Τοὺς φύλακας οὓς εἶπον περιστήσαντες, χρόνον ῥητὸν ὁρίσαντες ἑαυτοῖς πρὸς διόρθωσιν, καὶ καταδίκην ἐπιθέντες, εἰ τοῦ χρόνου παρελθόντος μὴ κατορθώσαιμεν τοῦτο. Πόσος οὖν ἡμῖν χρόνος ἀρκέσει πρὸς τοῦτο; Οὐκ οἶμαι τοὺς σφόδρα νήφοντας καὶ διεγηγερμένους καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἀγρυπνοῦντας σωτηρίας πλέον ἡμερῶν δέκα δεηθήσεσθαι, ὥστε παντελῶς ἀπαλλαγῆναι τῆς πονηρᾶς τῶν ὅρκων συνηθείας.
thought_title: Habit, accountability, and a ten-day cure for oaths
orientation: Chrysostom is still addressing the catechumens about oaths, answering the objection that great saints sinned and prescribing practical steps to break the habit of swearing.
pass_a_gloss: He commanded, he says; it was necessary to obey, and not to put forward so-and-so, nor to busy oneself with others' evils. Since the great David sinned a grievous sin; is then for this reason sinning without danger for us, tell me? For this reason then it is necessary to secure this, and to emulate only the successes of the saints; but if somewhere there is carelessness and transgression of law, it is necessary to flee with much zeal. For the account is not with our fellow servants, but with the Master, and to him we will give the penalties of all the things we have lived. Let us prepare then for that tribunal; for even if ten thousand times admirable and great is the one who transgresses this law, he will pay entirely the punishment laid down for the transgression; for God is not a respecter of persons. How then is it possible and in what manner to flee the sin? For it is necessary not only to show that the charge is grievous, but also to advise how we might be freed. Do you have a wife, do you have a household slave, do you have children, and a friend, and a relative, and a neighbor? To all these entrust the guard over these matters. Is habit difficult, and terrible at tripping up, and hard to guard against, and does it often throw us in unwillingly and without knowing? Therefore by as much as you know the power of habit, by so much be eager to be freed from the evil habit, and transfer yourself to the other, the most useful one. For just as now when you were eager and guarding and anxious and taking thought, that habit was strong enough often to trip you up, so if you transfer yourself to the good habit of not swearing, you will be able never to fall into the falls of oaths, neither unwillingly nor carelessly; for habit is truly great, and has the power of nature. In order then that we may not toil continually, let us transfer ourselves to another habit, and ask this favor of each of those who are with you and associate with you, that he advise and exhort to flee oaths, and convict you when caught. For the guard that comes from them to you is also for them advice and exhortation toward the success. For the one who accuses another about oaths will not easily himself fall into this pit; for frequent swearing is no ordinary pit, not only when it happens about the smallest matters, but also when it happens about the greatest matters. But we, both buying vegetables and quarreling over two obols, and being angry at household slaves and threatening, call on God everywhere as witness; and a free man, one who has a share of some bare dignity, you would not have dared to call as witness in the marketplace over such matters, but even if you attempt it, you will pay the penalty for the insult; but the King of the heavens, the Master of the angels, both about purchases, and about money, and about chance matters when conversing, you drag into testimony; and how are these things bearable? From where then might we be freed from this evil habit? Having set around us the guards whom I mentioned, having defined for ourselves a fixed time for correction, and having imposed a penalty, if after the time has passed we should not accomplish this. How much time then will suffice for us for this? I do not think that those who are very sober and awake and keeping vigil over their own salvation will need more than ten days, so as to be completely freed from the evil habit of oaths.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'oaths' for ὅρκοι, and Chrysostom is forbidding all swearing.
The passage is about the power of habit; 'habit' captures the repeated practice Chrysostom describes.
Chrysostom uses the image of a pit into which one falls; 'pit' preserves the spatial metaphor.
The compound means 'much-oath-taking'; 'frequent swearing' conveys the repeated act Chrysostom condemns.
This is the traditional English rendering of the biblical term, and Chrysostom is echoing the biblical phrase.
The verb means to cause to stumble or trip; 'trip up' keeps the physical image of habit causing a fall.

bible_refs.note: οὐ γάρ ἐστι προσωπολήπτης ὁ Θεός

pass_b_english: He commanded, you say, and you should have obeyed, not use so-and-so as an excuse or busy yourself with other people's sins. The great David committed a serious sin. Does that make sinning safe for us? Tell me. For this very reason we must be on our guard and emulate only the successes of the saints. Wherever there is carelessness and transgression of the law, we must flee from it with all diligence. Our account is not with our fellow servants but with the Master, and to him we will give account for everything we have done in life. Let us prepare for that tribunal. Even if the one who breaks this law is a thousand times admirable and great, he will certainly pay the punishment laid down for the transgression, for God is no respecter of persons.

How then, and in what way, can we escape this sin? It is not enough to show that the charge is serious; I must also advise you how to be freed from it. Do you have a wife, a servant, children, a friend, a relative, a neighbor? Entrust the guarding of this matter to all of them. Habit is a hard thing, terrible at tripping us up, hard to guard against, and it often throws us in against our will and without our knowing it. So the more you know the power of habit, the more eagerly you should free yourself from the evil habit and move yourself over to the other one, the most useful one. Just as now, even when you are eager and on guard and anxious and careful, that habit has often managed to trip you up, so if you move yourself over to the good habit of not swearing oaths, you will never be able to fall into the pitfalls of oaths, even unwillingly or carelessly. Habit is truly a great thing and has the power of nature.

So that we do not labor constantly, let us move ourselves over to another habit, and ask this favor of each person who associates with you and spends time with you: that they counsel and urge you to flee from oaths, and convict you when you are caught. For the guard they keep over you is also counsel and exhortation for them toward this success. The one who accuses another about oaths will not easily fall into this pit himself. For frequent swearing is no ordinary pit—not only when it happens about the smallest matters, but also when it happens about the greatest. But we, buying vegetables and quarreling over two obols, angry with servants and threatening them, call on God as witness everywhere. You would not dare to call a free man, one who holds some empty honor, as witness in the marketplace over such matters; if you tried, you would pay the penalty for insult. But the King of the heavens, the Lord of the angels—when you are talking about purchases and money and ordinary things, you drag him in as witness. How can this be endured?

How then can we be freed from this evil habit? By stationing around ourselves the guards I mentioned, setting a fixed time for correction, and imposing a penalty on ourselves if we have not succeeded when the time has passed. How much time will be enough for this? I do not think that those who are very sober and awake and keeping watch over their own salvation will need more than ten days to be completely freed from the evil habit of oaths.

problems.quote: imitate only the successes of the saints
problems.source_quote: τὰ κατορθώματα τῶν ἁγίων μόνον ζηλοῦν
problems.why: ζηλοῦν means 'emulate/zealously imitate', not 'imitate only'; μόνον modifies κατορθώματα, not ζηλοῦν
problems.fix: emulate only the successes of the saints

problems.quote: Does that make sinning safe for us? Tell me. No—for this very reason
problems.source_quote: ἆρα οὖν ἀκίνδυνον ἡμῖν διὰ τοῦτο τὸ ἁμαρτάνειν, εἰπέ μοι; Διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν τοῦτο ἀσφαλίζεσθαι χρή
problems.why: Source has no 'No—'; answer is positive: 'for this very reason we must be on our guard,' not a negation.
problems.fix: Tell me, does that make sinning safe for us? For this very reason we must be on our guard
problems.ruling: Διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν τοῦτο ἀσφαλίζεσθαι χρή: 'for this very reason we must guard ourselves' — positive exhortation, not 'No—' negation. Translator added false negative.

fixed: Changed 'imitate only' to 'emulate only' to reflect ζηλοῦν as 'emulate'.

problems.fix: not use so-and-so as an excuse
problems.ruling: προβάλλεσθαι with accusative person means 'put forward as excuse/pretext'; 'put forward' alone misses the excuse sense.

problems.ruling: εὐθύνας means 'account/reckoning,' not 'penalties'; changes meaning from giving account to paying penalties.

problems.ruling: ψιλῆς ἀξίας = 'mere/empty honor'; 'small office' misleads reader into thinking of a minor post, not honorary title.

last_rejected.quote: not use so-and-so as an excuse
last_rejected.why: προβάλλεσθαι means 'put forward as a shield/screen', not 'use as excuse'; the sense is using someone else as a cover for oneself.
last_rejected.fix: not put someone else forward as a screen
last_rejected.ruling: προβάλλεσθαι can mean 'put forward as pretext/shield'; 'use as excuse' captures this adequately.

last_rejected.quote: busy yourself with other people's sins
last_rejected.why: ἀλλότρια κακά means 'others' evils/sufferings' as things not one's own concern; 'busy yourself' is too active, and 'sins' narrows κακά.
last_rejected.fix: nor meddle in evils that are another's concern
last_rejected.ruling: κακά can mean 'sins/evils'; περιεργάζεσθαι 'busy oneself with' is standard; meaning preserved.

last_rejected.why: Glossary specifies 'ὅρκοι' = 'oaths', banned 'swearing'; but 'swearing oaths' uses banned term. Should be 'not taking oaths' or 'not using oaths'.
last_rejected.ruling: No glossary provided in source; 'swearing oaths' is normal English for ὀμνύναι; no evidence of ban.

last_rejected.why: πολυορκία means 'much-oath-taking, multiplicity of oaths', not 'frequent swearing'; 'swearing' is banned per glossary (ὅρκοι = oaths, banned 'swearing').
last_rejected.ruling: No glossary provided; πολυορκία = frequent oath-taking, 'frequent swearing' is standard English equivalent.
